newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean crop a record, corn fourth-largest.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean crop a record, corn fourth-largest.

text.p: U.S. farmers will reap their largest soybean crop ever, a mammoth 2.74 billion bushels, the government forecast on Tuesday in its first estimate of the fall harvest.

The Agriculture Department pegged corn at 9.28 billion bushels, the fourth-largest on record despite dry weather that cut into the crop. Blessed by record yields, the wheat crop was estimated at 2.53 billion bushels, 11 percent larger than last year, and cotton was pegged at 17.8 million bales, 6 percent lower than 1996.

Abundant crops would allow an easing in prices and a slight rebuilding of U.S. stockpiles without diminishing the flood of exports or stinting the surging domstic appetite for food and grain. Lower grain and feed prices also might constrain meat prices, now edging upward.
Dry weather in late July brought some peril to corn and soybeans and reduced crop condition ratings. However, beneficial rains fell in the Midwest at the start of this week.
"If the rains are arriving, it (corn) will come back," said private consultant John Schnittker.

Lured by high prices this spring, farmers planted the largest corn and soybean acreage in 15 years, making bin-busting crops a near certainty. Some 80.2 million acres of corn and 70.9 million acres of soybeans were sown.
August is a key month as spring-planted crops near maturity. The August crop report is the first each year to be based on field surveys of those crops.

Soybean yields were forecast at 39.3 bushels an acre, up 1.7 from last year. A record winter wheat yield of 44.6 bushels an acre helped boost the overall U.S. wheat yield to a forecast 39.9 bushels an acre -- a record. Good weather boosted the outlook for durum wheat and spring wheat, now being harvested. Corn yields were estimated at 125.3 bushels an acre, about six bushels an acre lower than projected a month ago. Stalk counts were at record levels in the seven major growing states, suggesting large output, but in 18 other states yields were expected to be lower than last year.
The estimate was a quarter-billion bushels lower than expected by analysts.
